about.line: Prairieland is fictional; its numbers are illustrative.
about.what: Shared data of Prairieland, Learn's national scale (S4, wave W6): five regions, the 2025 energy balance, the supply fleet with vintages, transmission, imports and minerals, the battery factory, fixed cost ranges, the carbon budget, time slices for engine E4, shocks and demand scenarios. Read by F10, A20, A21, M13, SB4 (engine E4) and C4; pages read these numbers and never retype them.
about.fictional: Prairieland is fictional. Its card (people, primary energy and shares, imports, Ridge County) is the course's own; costs come from EIA's 2026 assumptions; hourly shapes from SPP's 2025 grid; CO2 factors from the IPCC. Everything else is set for teaching and labelled so in the builder.
about.builtBy: scripts/build_learn_prairieland.py (ResearchPortfolio repository): python3 scripts/build_learn_prairieland.py --site <site>; tested by _tests/learn/test_prairieland.js
about.method: Top-down from the card: primary energy 3.5 EJ split by its shares, then refinery, power plants and grid to final energy by sector and carrier, then useful energy; the fleet's generation unit by unit; regions by teaching weights that add up to the nation exactly. Time slices from SPP's 2025 hourly shapes, 12 slices with the peak net-load day and the scarce-wind winter week kept whole.
simplifications: All fossil energy is counted as burned (no non-energy use such as plastics or asphalt).
One demand shape (SPP's 2025) serves every region; regions differ in size, not in daily shape.
Wind in each region is the same 2025 shape shifted by a lag and scaled; solar is scaled.
Transmission is a transport model: transfer limits, no power-flow physics.
No exports, no international bunkers, no biomass: the card's five sources make all primary energy.

units.energy: PJ on net calorific values unless a key says TWh, GWh or MWh
units.power: MW unless a key says GW
units.co2: Mt CO2 unless a key says t

nation.set: card: people, GDP, primary energy and its shares, the import shares, the CO2 total; teaching: the split of renewables, the workforce (A13's), everything derived below

regions.name: Northern Highlands
regions.story: Rivers and reservoirs: most of the nation's hydro, an aluminium smelter, few people.

regions.name: Ridge
regions.story: Ridge County's coal mines, Ridge Station and the steel and cement works; wind on the ridges.

regions.name: Western Plains
regions.story: The best wind, farms and oil and gas fields; far from the big loads.

regions.name: Capital Valley
regions.story: The capital and most of the factories, the battery industry among them; the largest load.

climate.kind: continental: cold winters, hot summers (Prairie City's climate)

regions.name: South Coast
regions.story: The port beyond the strait: the oil terminal, the refinery and the LNG terminal; offshore crude; the most sun.

balance.basis: net calorific values; physical energy content method

useful.note: Useful energy, a teaching convention: heat delivered by furnaces and boilers, motion from engines (30%) and EVs (89%) (DOE's figures, read from prairie-city.json); electricity's other uses count at 100% by convention. Heat pumps are few in 2025, so no outdoor heat is shown.

sankey.note: Prairieland's 2025 energy flows in PJ, rounded to 0.1 PJ; every node balances exactly (each node's loss link is the rounded remainder). Physical energy content method on net calorific values: nuclear enters as reactor heat, of which two thirds is lost in the power plants; hydro, wind and solar enter as electricity.

conventions.note: physicalContent (used here; the IEA's method): nuclear counts as the heat its reactors make (electricity / 0.33), hydro, wind and solar as their electricity. substitution: every MWh of electricity from nuclear, hydro, wind and solar counts as the fossil fuel a thermal plant would have burned to make it, here at Prairieland's own fossil fleet efficiency (41.8%): renewables' share rises from 10% to 21.2%. directEquivalent: all of them at their electricity output. Fossil fuels are the same in all three. Never compare primary shares across sources without checking the method.

balance.set: teaching: refinery losses 5.5%, gas own use 3%, mines' own use 10 PJ, grid losses 6%, the sector splits and useful-energy efficiencies; derived: everything else

fleet.note: Set for teaching: units, sizes, years built, efficiencies (net calorific values) and the 2025 capacity factors of the fuel plants (coal 62%, combined cycle 38%, turbines 8%, oil 5%). Derived: nuclear output from the card's 5% of primary energy (heat x 0.33), hydro from the card's 10% less wind and solar, wind and solar from each region's capacity factor. A unit retires at the end of its retire year (built + life unless set). Ridge Station's 2,400 MW is A13's.

expansion.set: teaching: new transmission in 2025 dollars per MW of transfer limit per km, lines and substations together

transmission.note: Set for teaching: existing links between regions, their transfer limits (MW, either way) and lengths; losses 1% per 100 km. A transport model: flows obey the limits, not the laws of power flow.

oil.route: All imported crude arrives by sea through one strait, then at the South Coast's oil terminal and refinery.
oil.benchmarkNote: IEA members that import oil hold stocks of at least 90 days of their net imports; Prairieland holds 60 (set for teaching), below that benchmark.

lng.note: Set for teaching: a quarter of the LNG cargoes also pass the strait; gas storage holds 15% of a year's gas use.

coal.note: All coal is mined in Ridge County and moved by rail to plants and works in other regions.

dependence.method: Import dependence = net imports / primary energy (Eurostat's indicator divides by gross available energy; here the two are the same, with no exports or bunkers). E4's import-share cap uses the same ratio in each period.

minerals.hhiMethod: Herfindahl-Hirschman index: the sum of each supplier's squared percentage share (0 to 10,000); above 1,800 counts as highly concentrated under the 2023 U.S. Merger Guidelines (DOJ and FTC; 2,500 under the 2010 guidelines). 'Other refiners' is one group, counted as a single supplier, so the index is a lower bound.
minerals.set: teaching: shares and tonnes per GWh (a mixed fleet of battery chemistries; real intensities vary by chemistry); the leading refiner's average share is set near the IEA's figure for 2025 (about 70%)

factories.note: A battery-cell factory in Capital Valley (set for teaching): its refined minerals come from abroad, most from Country R; output, jobs, electricity and stocks are illustrative.

firm.label: Firm clean plant (generic)

source.where: Table 4, the firm low-carbon plants that burn no fuel, from about $2,700 to $11,600 per kW; Prairieland's one generic option spans that range, and its fixed O&M ($150 per kW-year) lies inside Table 3's range for the same plants.

firm.what: One generic firm clean option: steady output up to 90% of its size in every slice, no CO2 in operation, the same constant cost in every period, the generic build limits of every technology. It stands for any firm low-carbon plant, not one design. Variable cost $9 per MWh, availability and life set for teaching.

anchor.what: average cost of gas to U.S. power plants, 2025 (EIA), via e2-plains-grid.json
average cost of coal to U.S. power plants, 2025 (EIA), via e2-plains-grid.json

oil.label: Crude oil
oil.note: About $70 a barrel at about 5.8 GJ a barrel (rounded); the range is roughly $40 to $130 a barrel.

fuels.note: Dollars per GJ on net calorific values (the balance's basis). EIA's prices are per MMBtu on gross heating values: x 1/1.055056 GJ per MMBtu and / 0.90 (gas) or / 0.95 (coal) for net values (IEA's convention, rounded). The ranges are set for teaching; each is what a learner may set, constant over the periods unless a shock changes it.

buildLimits.also: wind and solar also stop at each region's windMaxGW and solarMaxGW
buildLimits.set: teaching: generic limits, the same rule in every region and period; no technology has its own timeline

costs.rule: Every cost is a fixed range the learner sets, the same in every period; no cost changes with how much is built. Defaults are EIA's Table 3 values (2025 dollars); each range lies inside its source's range (`source`).
costs.note: Capital in 2025 dollars per kW (battery: per kW of a 4-hour battery), fixed O&M per kW-year, variable O&M per MWh. Annualised at the discount rate (periods.discount) over each life.

presets.label: A straight line to zero in 2050
A straight line to zero in 2040

budget.set: teaching: the budget is a learner choice; the presets are arithmetic on 2025's emissions, not a fair share

accounting.method: Cumulative CO2 2026-2050 = sum over the model years of weight x that year's emissions (Mt a year). linear: yearly emissions move in a straight line between model years, so 2026-2030 count 2 x 2025 + 3 x 2030, and so on (weights 2, 5, 5, 5, 5, 3; they sum to 25 years). step: each model year's emissions count for the five years ending in it (weights 0, 5, 5, 5, 5, 5).
accounting.boundary: Energy CO2 inside Prairieland: fuels burned (all counted as burned, no non-energy use), refinery and field own use; imported electricity none; methane and other gases left out.

carbon.context: For scale: 214.9 Mt is about 0.6% of the world's energy CO2 of about 38 Gt in 2025 (IEA), while Prairieland holds about 0.25% of the world's people. A recent peer-reviewed estimate puts the remaining global budget for a 50% chance of 1.5 C at about 130 Gt from the start of 2026 (Forster et al. 2026); how a nation's share is set is a choice (lesson A20).

periods.note: Model years 2030, 2035, 2040, 2045 and 2050, each standing for five years; 2025 is the observed base year. The same 12 time slices (weather of 2025) are used in every period; demand scales them.
periods.residualValue: Assets whose lives run past 2050 keep a residual value: E4 charges each plant's yearly capital payments (annuities at the discount rate over its life) only for the years up to 2050, so a plant built in 2045 pays for 2045-2050 only.
periods.retirement: Each existing unit retires at the end of its `retire` year (fleet.units); E4 may retire coal and gas earlier, saving their fixed O&M; existing plants' capital is sunk.
periods.foresight: Perfect foresight: one LP over 2030-2050. Decade by decade (myopic): solve 2030 and 2035 seeing only them, fix their builds, then 2040 and 2045, then 2050 (M13 compares the two).

hourRule.index: town_year.json index i (0 to 8759): day i // 24 of 2025 and hour i % 24, Central standard time (no clock change).
hourRule.season: winter December-February, spring March-May, summer June-August, autumn September-November (by the day's month).
hourRule.part: day: hours 08 to 19; night: hours 20 to 07.
hourRule.extremes: the 7 days of the scarce-wind winter week and the peak net-load day are taken out of their seasons and kept as their own slices.
hourRule.demand: every region's hourly load = its yearly electricity at the busbar (final + its grid losses) / 8760 x demand[i] / mean(demand): one shape for all regions, SPP's 2025.
hourRule.wind: region r's wind per MW in hour i = windScale[r] x wind[(i - windLagHours[r]) mod 8760] / 1000 (the SPP shape, shifted by the lag, scaled so the year's mean is the region's capacity factor).
hourRule.solar: region r's solar per MW in hour i = solarScale[r] x solar[i] / 1000 (scaled, not shifted).
hourRule.hydro: a season factor (set for teaching: winter 0.75, spring 1.35, summer 1.10, autumn 0.80), scaled so the hour-weighted mean over the year is 1; hydro output in a slice = hydro GW x hydroCF x factor.
hourRule.slice: a slice's demand, wind and solar are the means over its hours of the hourly values above; its weight is its number of hours.

scarceWindWeek.rule: the 7 whole days inside January-February or inside December with the least wind output of the 2025 fleet, all regions together

peakNetLoadDay.rule: the day of the year's highest hourly national net load (load at the busbar less the 2025 fleet's wind and solar), outside the scarce-wind week

chronology.weights: Each slice's hours; they sum to 8,760.
chronology.days: A season's day and night slices form one representative day (12 + 12 hours) that stands for `days` days; batteries cycle within it (end of night = start of day).
chronology.week: The scarce-wind week is 7 consecutive days: a store may enter it full but must cover the week's shortfall from what it holds (no refill from other seasons).
chronology.extremes: Kept whole: the peak net-load day and the scarce-wind winter week.
chronology.sameYear: Load, wind, solar and the hydro factor all come from one weather year (2025), so their correlation survives.
chronology.outages: Forced outages are left out of the planning LP (availability factors stand in); adequacy is never judged from slices (lesson A5).

weatherYears.role: the year the slices come from
an independent weather year (29 February left out)

fullYearCheck.method: Fix the plan's capacities in each checked period and re-dispatch them hour by hour over the full year by the hourRule (2024: the same rule with that year's shapes, the same windScale and solarScale, so its capacity factors differ by weather), with transmission limits and storage linked hour to hour.
report: CO2 of the year against the slice estimate
hours each link is at its limit
the scarce-wind week's lowest store level
fullYearCheck.survives: Set for teaching: a conclusion survives if it holds in both years: all demand served, CO2 within 10% of the slice estimate, the same ranking of plans. A plan that fails the 2024 year is reported, not hidden.

shocks.label: Gas-price spike
shocks.what: LNG costs 3 times its price and domestic gas 1.5 times, for one model year the learner picks (default 2030).

shocks.label: Drought
shocks.what: Hydro output 35% lower in every slice of one model year; thermal plants cooled by rivers lose 10% of their capacity in the summer slices.

shocks.label: Mineral export restriction
shocks.what: Country R stops exports of refined battery minerals for two years: the factory runs on other suppliers, recycling and its stock; new batteries cost 1.5 times as much in that model year.

shocks.label: Demand surprise
shocks.what: Electricity demand 10% above the scenario in every slice from 2035 (new large loads, data centers among them, and faster electrification), not known when the earlier periods are planned.

shocks.label: Strait closure
shocks.what: Ships cannot pass the strait for 8 weeks: all crude imports and a quarter of LNG cargoes stop.

shocks.label: Factory fire
shocks.what: The battery factory stops for 6 months; batteries must be imported at a premium of 20%.

demand.method: growth: % a year in each sector's useful energy (the services: heat, motion, light), from 2025; newLoadsTWh: extra electricity a year from new large loads (factories and data centers, loads only), straight-line between the years shown.

buildings.what: heat pumps, seasonal COP 3, against gas and oil furnaces at 80%

transport.what: EVs (89%) against engines (30%): DOE's figures, read from prairie-city.json

industry.what: a mix of electric boilers and industrial heat pumps for heat below about 400 C; a 1.5 ratio of useful heat per unit of electricity

electrification.set: teaching: ratios are useful energy per unit of final energy; at most 15 percentage points of a sector's useful energy can switch to electricity per period; industry at most 60% by 2050; end-use equipment costs are left out

demand.realWorld: For comparison: EIA's AEO2026 cases put U.S. electricity use growing 0.9% to 1.6% a year to 2050 (a spread of cases, not a forecast range).

a13.note: Ridge County is Prairieland's coal-dependent county (curriculum v2 §6, scale S4). A13 sets its numbers here and wave W6 (SB4, C4) reuses them: change them together with W6. Anchors from the national-strategy dossier §8.0: Prairieland has 20 million people; Ridge County holds 3% of its workforce; coal provides 40% of the county's local tax revenue. Everything else is set for teaching.
a13.fiction: Ridge County and Prairieland are fictional; their numbers are illustrative.
a13.set: teaching: the workforce, the county's tax revenue other than the plant's ($840M a year, of which $300M is paid by the coal mines), the plant's size, staff, taxable value and the mine jobs that supply it

ridgeCounty.note: Ridge County lies in the Ridge region. Its numbers are A13's, copied whole and unchanged in `a13` (a change goes to A13's data and here together). All of Prairieland's coal is mined there: 27.1 Mt a year at IPCC's 25.8 TJ per kt.
